metadata.title: CoACL: Coupled Augmentation for Contrastive Learning on Text-Attributed Graphs Under Semantic Supervision from Large Language Models
metadata.abstract_summary: This paper proposes CoACL, a framework that uses LLM semantic supervision to denoise structural and textual information and alleviate data sparsity in text-attributed graphs. CoACL consistently outperforms strong baselines and yields up to 7.1% absolute improvement in node classification.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text: Text-attributed graphs (TAGs) couple graph topology with node-level text, but real data often contain spurious edges, missing links, and text–structure mismatch that destabilize learning under scarce labels. We propose CoACL (Coupled Augmentation for Contrastive Learning), a framework that uses LLM semantic supervision to denoise structural and textual information and alleviate data sparsity. CoACL first prunes the candidate edge space using structural similarity and then queries an LLM to discard suspicious edges and confirm plausible links, yielding semantically consistent positive and negative pairs. We further introduce keyword-focused text augmentations and learn coupled representations by optimizing a joint text–graph contrastive objective guided by semantics. Experiment results on Cora, PubMed, and the Open Graph Benchmark Arxiv dataset (OGBN-Arxiv) show that CoACL consistently outperforms strong baselines and yields up to 7.1% absolute improvement in node classification accuracy, with the largest gains in low-label regimes. By constraining LLM evaluation to similarity-based candidates, CoACL targets neighborhood- level noise with controlled cost.

claims.text: CoACL, a framework that uses LLM semantic supervision to denoise structural and textual information and alleviate data sparsity, is proposed.
CoACL consistently outperforms strong baselines and yields up to 7.1% absolute improvement in node classification accuracy, with the largest gains in low-label regimes.
CoACL targets neighborhood-level noise with controlled cost by constraining LLM evaluation to similarity-based candidates.
CoACL uses keyword-focused text augmentations and learns coupled representations by optimizing a joint text-graph contrastive objective guided by semantics.

sections.heading: Keywords:
sections.text: text-attributed graphs; graph contrastive learning; large language models; semantics-aware augmentation; noise correction 1. Introduction Graphs are a fundamental form of structured data and arise in a wide range of applications. In many real-world graphs, nodes are associated with textual attributes. For example, ogbn-products from the Open Graph Benchmark (OGB) is an e-commerce product graph in which each node represents a product and its textual description serves as the node attribute. In graph learning, graphs equipped with node-level text are commonly referred to as Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) [ 1 ]. Recent evidence also suggests that directly applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to graph analysis remains challenging, motivating principled integration of LLM semantics with graph learning [ 2 ]. Text-Attributed Graph Learning (TAGL), which lies at the intersection of Graph Rep- resentation Learning (GRL) and Natural Language Processing (NLP), has been widely Electronics 2026 , 15 , 844 https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15040844 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 844 2 of 22 adopted in real-world applications. TAGL aims to jointly exploit graph topology and tex- tual semantics, enabling more expressive modeling than unimodal graph-only or text-only approaches. In social network analysis, incorporating user relations and textual content (e.g., tweets and comments) is effective for tasks such as fake-account (bot) detection and community detection [ 3 ]. In recommender systems, jointly modeling product descriptions and user–item interaction graphs can alleviate data sparsity and improve recommenda- tion quality [ 4 , 5 ]. In biomedical knowledge discovery, integrating scientific text with drug–target interaction networks has facilitated drug repositioning prediction [ 6 ]. These applications suggest that topology and semantics provide complementary signals in TAGL. From a modeling perspective, textual attributes provide node-level semantic cues that can be encoded by LLMs, while graph structure captures relational proximity and homophily that can be modeled by Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) via message passing. Beyond local propagation, recent studies also explore structural information measures to characterize global organization and uncertainty in graphs under weak or noisy supervision [ 7 ]. Motivated by the complementarity between semantic and structural information, recent TAGL methods increasingly integrate LLMs and GNNs in a co-training paradigm. However, in real-world TAGs, noisy edges and ambiguous text can lead to misalignment between semantic and structural signals, yielding unreliable supervision and degraded representations. Despite substantial progress, the effectiveness of TAGL is still limited by two pervasive challenges in real-world scenarios: noise interference and data sparsity. Existing TAGL methods improve downstream performance via joint modeling of text and topology [ 8 ], while topology-aware contrastive learning further treats textual and structural views as complementary for representation learning [ 9 ]. First, many contrastive designs still un- deruse contextualized text semantics, relying on bag-of-words signals or shallow text encoders that are insufficient for fine-grained semantic discrimination. Second, common structural perturbations, such as random edge masking or topology-only edits, are often imposed without semantic constraints, undermining text–structure consistency. Third, connectivity-driven negative sampling can misclassify semantically related nodes as nega- tives, inducing false negatives and weakening separability, which in turn hampers stable contrastive optimization [ 10 , 11 ]. To address these limitations, we propose CoACL (Coupled Augmentation for Con- trastive Learning on Text-Attributed Graphs), an LLM-supervised coupled augmentation framework that denoises both graph structure and node text for robust contrastive learn- ing. Implementation Details Unless otherwise specified, we repeat each experiment three times with different random seeds and report the mean ± standard deviation over the three runs. The max- imum number of training epochs is set to 100 with early stopping based on validation accuracy. We optimize all models using Adam with a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 3 and a mini-batch size of 32. For hyperparameter selection, we search the candidate set size K in { 2, 6, 8, 10, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 } , and the coupling loss weights λ and γ in { 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 } . For the LLM-based semantic evaluation in the noise-correction module, we use ChatGLM-130B . For LLM-based baselines, we initialize the encoder with bert-base-uncased . https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15040844 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 844 11 of 22 To ensure fair comparison, all baseline methods and CoACL are trained and eval- uated using exactly the same preprocessed node texts. No baseline is provided with additional textual information or alternative preprocessing beyond the standardized pipeline described above. 4.1.2. Datasets To comprehensively evaluate the effectiveness of CoACL, we conduct node classifica- tion on three real-world text-attributed graph datasets: Cora [ 30 ], OGBN-Arxiv [ 12 ], and PubMed [ 30 ]. For all datasets, we apply a unified text preprocessing pipeline to ensure consistency and fairness across methods. The pipeline includes lowercasing, removal of non- informative symbols, normalization of whitespace, and truncation to a fixed maximum length. To ensure fair comparison, all baseline methods and CoACL are trained and evaluated using exactly the same preprocessed node texts. No baseline is provided with additional textual information or alternative preprocessing beyond the standardized pipeline described above. sections.heading: Cora Dataset
sections.text: : This dataset is a widely used citation network in the field of machine learning, originally provided by Repositories Group. It contains 2708 scientific papers, each represented by a 1433-dimensional binary word vector indicating the presence or absence of specific terms in a vocabulary. Citation relationships between papers form 5429 edges, creating a citation graph where papers are classified into seven categories. For the Cora dataset, additional cleaning is required because the original node text contains incomplete keyword lists and occasional formatting artifacts. Specifically, we remove duplicated keywords, filter malformed tokens, and complete missing textual fields when possible using the dataset-provided metadata. After preprocessing, all node texts are standardized into the same text-attributed graph format. •

Baselines We evaluate combinations of text encoders and GNN backbones for node classifica- tion on TAGs. The text encoder is chosen from shallow embeddings (SE; e.g., Bag-of- Words (BoW)) [ 13 ], a frozen language model (LLM-plain), a fine-tuned language model https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15040844 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 844 12 of 22 (LLM-tune), and GIANT, a recently proposed TAG learning baseline that enhances node representations with external textual signals. The GNN backbone is selected from Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) [ 16 ], Graph Attention Network (GAT) [ 17 ], and GraphSAGE (SAGE) [ 18 ]. For CoACL, we use ChatGLM-130B to provide LLM-based semantic supervision in the augmentation modules. For baselines that require dense text embeddings (e.g., LLM-plain and LLM-tune), we use BERT-base-uncased [ 31 , 32 ] to obtain initial text representations. •

Compared with the strongest baseline in each setting, CoACL improves node classification accuracy by roughly 3–8%, with the largest gains appearing under noisier or lower-label regimes. These results suggest that jointly con- trasting text and structure, together with semantics-aware augmentation, better captures complementary information in TAGs and improves robustness to noise. CoACL is also robust in low-label regimes. On Cora, when the labeling ratio decreases from 10% to 1%, CoACL drops from 86.2 to 78.2, while the strongest baseline (LLM-tune with GCN) decreases from 83.8 to 74.4; CoACL therefore preserves a 3.8-point advantage under 1% labels. Similar robustness is observed on PubMed and OGBN-Arxiv, where CoACL improves the best baseline by 3.1 and 4.6 points under 1% labeling, respectively. This robustness stems https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15040844 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 844 14 of 22 from the coupled augmentation strategy, which strengthens view consistency and reduces the impact of noisy neighborhoods during contrastive optimization. 4.3. Ablation Study The CoACL model consists of three core components: noise correction, node attribute augmentation and graph structure augmentation based on the LLM. In order to deeply analyze the impact of each component on the model performance and comprehensively reveal the working principle of the model, a series of meticulous ablation experiments are carried out in our method. All ablation experiments are conducted using the same prepro- cessed text as in the main experiments, ensuring that observed performance differences are caused by architectural or objective-function changes rather than text quality variations. Effect of LLM-Based Noise Correction The results of the ablation experiment to assess the effectiveness of the noise correction mechanism based on the LLM for TAGL are shown in Figure 2 . Figure 2. Effectiveness of CoACL noise correction mechanism based on large language model on three datasets. In all three datasets, with the increase in the proportion of labeled data, the classifi- cation accuracies of both methods show a rising trend, but the CoACL method always outperforms the method that only uses the first-order neighbors (1-hop neighbors), which fully verifies the effectiveness of the noise correction mechanism based on the LLM. Specifi- cally, in the Arxiv dataset, the classification accuracy of the CoACL method is improved by about 4 to 7 percentage points compared with that of the 1-hop neighbors method, while in the PubMed dataset, although the overall improvement is relatively small, it still reaches 2 to 4 percentage points, which indicates that the noise-correction mechanism has a positive impact on the performance of the model. Notably, in the Cora dataset, the CoACL method demonstrates the most significant improvement in accuracy, with an overall improvement of 6–12 percentage points, which further highlights its advantage in the high-noise envi- ronment. Conventional graph contrastive learning methods typically rely on generic augmentations (e.g., node dropping, edge perturbation, and subgraph sampling), which can distort graph semantics and introduce representation bias. By contrast, CoACL uses LLM-guided semantic evidence to refine candidate relations, leading to more stable and informative message propagation. 4.3.4. All other components, including LLM-based noise correction and coupled augmentations, are kept identical. This comparison aims to isolate the effect of explicitly penalizing semantically negative pairs beyond the implicit negative competition in InfoNCE. Parameter Sensitivity Three key parameters in the CoACL model: the length of the augmented candidate set K for the noise correction module based on the LLM, and the coupled loss weights λ and γ for the text and graph models in joint contrastive learning. In order to analyze in depth the extent to which each of the parameters affects the performance of the model, further experimental validation of its important parameters is carried out in our method. In Figure 4 , we report how the candidate-set size K affects training efficiency and CoACL performance. As K increases, accuracy improves rapidly at first and then saturates. For example, accuracy is 49.2% at K = 2 and peaks at 72.7% around K = 10 (a + 23.5% gain). Small K provides insufficient structural context, limiting representation learning and reducing the effectiveness of LLM-based correction. Increasing K supplies richer candidates and helps the LLM identify semantically consistent relations, but overly large K yields diminishing returns because the added candidates become less informative. Training time also increases with K . As the candidate set grows, the noise-correction module must score many more node pairs with the LLM, substantially increasing com- putational overhead. In practice, K ≈ 10 offers a good trade-off: it achieves near-optimal accuracy while keeping training cost within a reasonable range. We therefore set K = 10 in the LLM-based noise-correction module. https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15040844 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 844 17 of 22 Figure 4. Effect of parameter K on CoACL performance and training efficiency on Arxiv 10%. For the coupling-loss weights λ and γ , we evaluate different hyperparameter combi- nations on Cora with a 10% labeling rate. Figure 5 shows that setting λ = γ = 0 yields the lowest accuracy, confirming the importance of both coupling components. The best performance is achieved around λ = 1.5 (text weight) and γ = 1 (graph weight). Moreover, the presence of a broad high-performing region indicates that CoACL is not overly sensitive to moderate changes in these hyperparameters. Figure 5. Effect of coupling loss weights on Cora 10% γ and λ on CoACL performance and training efficiency. 4.5. Limitations and Practical Guidance LLM-based semantic supervision is most beneficial when the graph structure is noisy (e.g., spurious edges/missing links), textual attributes are ambiguous, or labeled data are scarce, where semantic reasoning can help correct false relations and reduce false negatives. In contrast, for relatively clean graphs with strong homophily and sufficient supervi- sion, simpler structural or contrastive approaches may already yield competitive perfor- mance, and LLM supervision can be optional. https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15040844 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 844 18 of 22 We also acknowledge several practical limitations: (i) potential privacy concerns when querying external LLM services with sensitive node texts, (ii) performance degradation under domain shifts (when text/style differs from the LLM’s training distribution), and (iii) occasional semantic errors introduced by imperfect LLM judgments. In practice, these issues can be mitigated by caching LLM outputs (offline preprocess- ing), restricting semantic evaluation to candidate subsets, and adopting smaller or local language models for privacy-sensitive or large-scale deployments; for high-stakes settings, lightweight human auditing can further improve reliability. 5. Conclusions We propose CoACL, an LLM-supervised coupled augmentation framework for con- trastive learning on text-attributed graphs. CoACL (i) narrows candidate relations via structural similarity

sections.heading: Example Prompt:
sections.text: Given a target paper node with the following textual description: Target node: “Probabilistic methods for information retrieval based on Bayesian inference.” Candidate paper nodes: 1. “A Bayesian framework for text classification and retrieval.” 2. “Neural network approaches to handwritten digit recognition.” 3. “Graph-based semi-supervised learning methods.” Please identify which candidate papers are most semantically related to the target paper in terms of research topic and content, and return the indices of the relevant nodes. Based on the constructed prompt, the LLM performs holistic semantic analysis over the candidate set. The output of the LLM is then used to distinguish semantically relevant neighbors from noisy connections. Appendix A.2. Deterministic Inference Settings To ensure stable and reproducible outputs, all experiments are conducted using a fixed prompt template and deterministic decoding settings. Specifically, the temperature is set to 0 and top-k to 1, thereby enforcing deterministic inference. Under this configuration, repeated runs with identical inputs produce consistent outputs. The same LLM checkpoint and inference configuration are used across all experiments to minimize additional sources of variability. Appendix A.3. Handling Noisy and Inconsistent Outputs LLMs may occasionally produce ambiguous or uncertain judgments in complex se- mantic reasoning tasks. To mitigate the impact of such behavior, a conservative filtering strategy is adopted. When the LLM output fails to clearly distinguish semantic relevance or exhibits insufficient confidence, the corresponding candidate edge is treated as a low- confidence connection and excluded from the refined graph structure. Furthermore, multiple independent inference runs are conducted on a subset of nodes to assess output consistency. The results demonstrate a high level of agreement across runs under fixed prompts and deterministic decoding settings, supporting the robustness of the proposed semantic supervision mechanism. It is important to note that the proposed method does not rely on fine-grained ranking scores or probability estimates produced by the LLM. Instead, it only leverages the LLM’s coarse-grained semantic discrimination capability over candidate connections, which fur- ther mitigates the impact of potential output variability on overall performance. https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15040844 Electronics 2026 , 15 , 844 20 of 22 Appendix A.4. Runtime Overhead and LLM Invocation Analysis In this subsection, we provide a brief analysis of the runtime overhead introduced by the LLM-based semantic supervision module, focusing on the number of LLM invocations and system-level time consumption. Table A1 summarizes the key runtime-related statistics of this module across different datasets, including the dataset name, number of processed nodes, neighborhood size K , average input and output token lengths, and the per-call LLM latency under deterministic decoding (temperature set to 0). For each target node n , the LLM is invoked once for each candidate set X ∈{N spu n , N ver n } . As shown in Table A1 , this design leads to a total number of LLM calls that grows linearly with the number of target nodes and remains independent of the neighborhood size K . Increasing K only affects the length of the input prompt, which is reflected in the average input token statistics reported in the table, rather than the frequency of LLM invocations. Table A1. claims.text: The 2023 4th International Conference on Computing, Networks and Internet of Things was held in Xiamen, China, from 26–28 May 2023.
The conference proceedings were published by the Association for Computing Machinery in New York, NY, USA.
Researchers have proposed various methods for traffic flow forecasting, including Contrastive-Learning-Based Adaptive Graph Fusion Convolution Network with Residual-Enhanced Decomposition Strategy.
Large Language Models (LLMs) have been explored for their potential in learning on graphs.
